title: A lake with no river
teaches: The landforms an ice sheet leaves behind, how shaded relief reveals them, and how the land rises once the ice is gone

parts.title: The footprint of an ice sheet

blocks.text: At the last glacial maximum, about 21,000 years ago, ice covered almost all of Canada and the northern edge of the United States. The Laurentide ice sheet, which grew from centres around Hudson Bay, was over 3 kilometres thick in places and reached south past the sites of New York, Chicago and Cincinnati. To the west, the smaller Cordilleran ice sheet filled the mountains of British Columbia and pushed a tongue of ice, the Puget lobe, south down the Puget Lowland past Seattle, where the ice stood about a kilometre thick.

blocks.caption: The northern ice sheets and the coastline over the last 130,000 years. The amount of ice, and with it the sea level, comes from the LR04 deep-sea record of lesson 14; the ice sheets' shapes are simplified, growing from their centres to their outlines at the last glacial maximum.
blocks.task: Play the last 130,000 years and watch the ice and the coastline

blocks.text: An ice sheet is a glacier on a continental scale, and it works on the ground in the same way as the Rhône glacier of lesson 13, only over millions of square kilometres. As it moves, it scrapes the bedrock, carries rock and soil along with it, and eventually drops them. Beneath the ice, it smears out a dense layer of unsorted clay, sand and boulders known as **till**. Out in front of the ice margin, meltwater streams spread sheets of **outwash**, sand and gravel sorted by running water in the same way the river sorted grains in lesson 2. When the ice finally melts away, it leaves a landscape that records how it moved and how it died.

Much of that record lies hidden under farm fields, forests and towns. Since the 2000s, however, aircraft carrying **lidar**, a laser rangefinder that fires hundreds of thousands of pulses a second, have mapped the bare ground of whole states to within a few centimetres by catching the pulses that slip through gaps in the tree canopy. When a computer shades that bare-earth model as if an imaginary sun were shining across it, landforms appear that people walking directly over them never noticed.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: About 21,000 years ago, ice sheets up to 3 km thick covered Canada and the northern United States, including the Puget Lowland.
Ice smears unsorted till (clay, sand and boulders) beneath its bed, while meltwater streams spread sorted outwash (sand and gravel) in front of it.
Airborne lidar measures the bare ground through tree cover, revealing glacial landforms that are hard to see from the ground.

blocks.text: Between Rochester and Syracuse in western New York, the farmland rolls over thousands of low, smooth hills that all point the same way. These are **drumlins**, from the Irish word *droimnín* (a little ridge): oval hills of till and older sediment, typically a kilometre or two long and a few tens of metres high, shaped like the back of a spoon. The New York drumlin field holds around 10,000 of them, making it one of the largest in the world. The Puget Lowland has them too, and Seattle's long north-to-south hills owe their shape to the same subglacial moulding.

blocks.caption: Chimney Bluffs on Lake Ontario, New York, where waves have cut into drumlins and exposed the sediment inside.

blocks.text: Drumlins form beneath moving ice, which shapes the sediment of its bed into streamlined ridges, much as a river shapes sand bars. They line up parallel to the ice flow, and most have a blunter, steeper end facing up-ice and a long tapering tail pointing down-ice. Geologists still debate the exact mechanics of how the ice builds and carves them, but a field of drumlins remains one of the clearest signs of which way an ice sheet moved.

blocks.caption: Shaded relief of farmland near Palmyra, New York, made from airborne lidar heights. Move the sun to light the ground from a different direction.
blocks.task: Light the drumlins so they stand out

blocks.text: This sensitivity to light direction is why shaded-relief maps let you move the sun. A slope facing the light looks bright, and a slope facing away sits in shadow. When light shines straight along a ridge, both flanks are lit equally and the feature almost vanishes; when light shines across the ridge, one flank catches the sun and the other falls into shadow, throwing the shape into relief. When geologists hunt for drumlins, old shorelines or **fault scarps** (the small steps a fault leaves where it breaks the surface, which we will meet in lesson 16), they cast light across the elevation model from several compass directions so that no trend gets lost in the glare.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Drumlins are streamlined hills of glacial sediment aligned with the ice flow, usually with a blunt up-ice end and a tapered down-ice tail.
On a shaded-relief map, elongated landforms stand out sharpest when lit at right angles to their long axes.

blocks.text: Many glaciated plains are pitted with small round lakes and dry hollows that have no stream flowing in or out. Walden Pond in Massachusetts is a **kettle** of this kind; Green Lake in Seattle is another. Each one marks the spot where a stranded block of glacier ice melted away.

blocks.caption: Walden Pond in Massachusetts, a kettle lake.

blocks.text: A shrinking ice sheet rarely retreats along a clean, tidy wall. Instead, its thinning margin breaks apart, leaving behind great blocks of dead ice detached from the main sheet. Meltwater streams pouring off the active ice bury these stranded blocks in outwash sand and gravel. Insulated under that blanket of sediment, a buried ice block can take decades or centuries to melt, and in permafrost regions thousands of years. As the ice slowly wastes away underground, the sand and gravel above slump into the void, leaving a steep-sided hollow at the surface. Where the bottom of the hollow dips below the **water table** (the depth below which the ground is saturated with water), groundwater seeps in through the permeable gravel to form a lake.

blocks.caption: How a kettle forms: a stranded block of ice is buried in outwash by meltwater, melts slowly underground, and leaves a hollow that fills with groundwater.

blocks.text: On central Whidbey Island in Washington, outwash plains pitted with large dry kettles form some of the island's best open farmland, explored in the Whidbey Island branch of this course. Wherever you find a cluster of kettles, you are looking at the graveyard of a stagnant, breaking ice margin.

blocks.caption: A kettle lake on the highlands of Isunngua, Greenland, with the ice sheet in the distance.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Kettles form when blocks of stagnant ice are buried in outwash sediment and later melt, causing the ground above to collapse.
Kettle lakes sit where a collapse hollow intersects the water table, fed and drained through the surrounding gravel.

blocks.text: An ice sheet is heavy enough to depress the rock beneath it. Lesson 5 described how continental crust floats on the denser mantle below, like a loaded barge in water. Add cargo to a barge and it sinks until it has displaced an equal weight of water. In the same way, crust loaded with ice sinks until it has pushed aside an equal weight of mantle rock. Because glacial ice is about 0.3 times as dense as mantle rock, an ice sheet 3 kilometres thick presses the crust down by roughly 900 metres, forcing the solid but ductile mantle beneath to flow slowly out of the way. Once the ice melts, the unloaded crust buoys back up, at a pace governed by how fast the viscous mantle can flow back underneath it.

blocks.caption: Crust floating on the mantle, weighed down by an ice sheet and rising after it melts. In this simplified model, as in reality, the rebound starts fast and slows over time.
blocks.task: Load the crust with at least 1.5 km of ice, melt it, and let at least 8,000 years pass

blocks.text: Around Hudson Bay, where the Laurentide ice was thickest, the land is still rising at more than a centimetre a year, over 8,000 years after the last of the ice melted away. Cobble beaches that waves cut at sea level just after the ice retreated have been lifted high onto the hillsides, forming staircase flights of old shorelines. Along Sweden's High Coast on the Gulf of Bothnia, where the Fennoscandian ice sheet once sat, the highest post-glacial shoreline now stands nearly 300 metres above the Baltic Sea. Around Puget Sound, marine clays and seashells laid down in cold salt water immediately after the ice lobe retreated now sit tens of metres above modern high tide, carried upward by the same post-glacial rebound.

blocks.caption: Hannah Bay, at the southern end of James Bay in Canada, seen from the Space Shuttle in winter. Snow picks out the ridges of old shorelines left behind as the land rose.

blocks.text: Even thousands of years after the ice sheets vanished, the crust is still recovering from their weight. The next lessons turn from these slow movements to sudden ones, where faults snap and coastlines drop in a matter of minutes.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Because ice has about 0.3 times the density of mantle rock, an ice sheet depresses the crust beneath it by roughly 0.3 times the ice thickness.
Once the ice melts, the crust rebounds over thousands of years as mantle rock flows back; the land around Hudson Bay still rises by more than 1 cm a year.
Flighted sequences of raised beaches and elevated marine sediments record how far the land has risen since deglaciation.

blocks.caption: Five questions on what the ice left
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: A drumlin has a steep, blunt north end and a long tail tapering to the south. Which way did the ice sheet move across this ground?
items.why: Drumlins typically have their blunt, steeper end facing up-ice and their tapered tail pointing down-ice, showing that the ice flowed from north to south.

items.ask: On a shaded-relief map, a swarm of ridges running north to south is barely visible. From which direction is the simulated sun most likely shining?
choices: From the north or south, parallel to the ridges
From the east or west, across the ridges
items.why: Light shining parallel to a ridge illuminates both of its flanks equally, producing almost no shadow contrast. Light shining across the ridge makes one flank bright and the other dark.

items.ask: How does a kettle lake form?
choices: A detached block of glacier ice buried in outwash melts, the sediment above collapses, and groundwater fills the resulting hollow
A meltwater river carves a plunge pool in bedrock beneath a subglacial waterfall
A ridge of till dams a valley stream after the glacier retreats
items.why: Kettles are collapse hollows left where blocks of stagnant ice were buried in outwash sand and gravel; when the bottom of the hollow reaches below the water table, groundwater fills it.

items.ask: An ice sheet 2 km thick sits on the continent for many thousands of years. Roughly how far does its weight depress the crust beneath it?
items.why: Glacial ice is about 0.3 times as dense as mantle rock, so at equilibrium the crust sinks by roughly 0.3 times the thickness of the ice load: 0.3 × 2,000 m = 600 m.

items.ask: Why is the land around Hudson Bay still rising today, more than 8,000 years after the Laurentide ice sheet melted?
choices: Solid mantle rock flows back beneath the unloaded crust very slowly, over thousands of years
Seasonal winter sea ice continues to depress and release the bay floor each year
Sediment carried by rivers into Hudson Bay is building up the coastline
items.why: Over geological timescales the solid mantle behaves like a very stiff fluid; after the ice load is removed, mantle rock takes many thousands of years to flow back and restore equilibrium.

summary: **Ice sheets leave distinct deposits.** Unsorted till beneath them, sorted outwash in front of them.
**Drumlins point the way the ice flowed.** They are moulded from sediment under the ice and aligned with its flow.
**Shaded relief reveals landforms.** Long features show best when lit across their length.
**Kettle lakes mark buried ice.** Blocks of stagnant ice in outwash melted, and the ground collapsed below the water table.
**Ice presses the land down.** An ice sheet sinks the crust by about 0.3 times its thickness.
**The land rises back slowly.** It rebounds over thousands of years as the mantle flows back.
